strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of current VLA policies: frame-wise visual processing without explicit temporal state. The proposed recurrent state plus Active Visual Attention module is well motivated for partially observable manipulation settings and is easy to integrate into an OpenVLA-OFT-style model.

The empirical evaluation is broad. Results are reported on LIBERO, CALVIN ABC-D, LIBERO+ perturbations, and Mobile ALOHA real-robot tasks. AVA-VLA improves over the OpenVLA-OFT baseline on LIBERO average SR from 96.8 to 98.0 in the all-suite setting and from 97.1 to 98.3 in the per-suite setting, and improves CALVIN average length from 4.10 to 4.65.

The ablations are useful: state-based initialization and the AVA module each improve the LIBERO all-suite average from 96.8 to 97.5, and their combination reaches 98.0. The backbone ablation on LIBERO-Long suggests the idea is not limited to one pretrained VLA backbone.

The qualitative visualizations and pruning study provide additional evidence that the learned visual weights capture task-relevant regions. Maintaining strong LIBERO performance after pruning 50-70% of visual tokens supports the claim that the weights are meaningful rather than merely decorative.
The manuscript is generally clear, with equations, architecture details, training settings, and appendix details sufficient to understand the main implementation choices.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat overstated. Maintaining recurrent hidden state for sequential decision-making is a standard response to partial observability, and the paper does not establish a strong theoretical link between the proposed hidden-state reuse and an actual belief-state approximation. The POMDP framing motivates the design but does not deeply constrain or validate it.

The reported improvements over the strongest baselines are often modest and no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multi-seed evaluations are provided. On benchmarks with already very high success rates, gains of about 1-2 points may be within evaluation variance, so the strength of the SOTA claim is hard to assess.

Many simulation baseline numbers are taken from prior papers rather than rerun under a unified protocol. This is common but leaves possible confounds in model size, data, training budget, evaluation episodes, and implementation details, especially for comparisons to recent 2025 systems.

The real-world evaluation is promising but limited: 24-30 trials per task and only two baselines. The baselines also appear to have different fine-tuning schedules, and there is no statistical analysis, failure taxonomy, or discussion of whether improvements come from temporal state, extra parameters, or additional training.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives useful hyperparameters, but it does not report random seeds, number of evaluation episodes for LIBERO/CALVIN, compute cost, parameter overhead, runtime latency, memory overhead, or whether code/checkpoints will be released. Important AVA details such as the projected dimension d' and sensitivity to gamma, c, lambda, and unroll length are not explored.

The method adds attention modulation to all LLM layers and recurrent processing, but efficiency is not analyzed despite the visual-token-pruning discussion. Without latency/memory measurements, it is unclear whether the approach is practical for high-rate real-time control beyond the reported tasks.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of current VLA policies: frame-wise visual processing is a poor fit for partially observed, temporally extended manipulation tasks.

The proposed recurrent-state-conditioned visual attention module is technically plausible and is integrated into a strong OpenVLA-OFT-style backbone with clear high-level equations and implementation details.

The evaluation covers several relevant settings: LIBERO, LIBERO+, CALVIN ABC->D, and Mobile ALOHA real-robot tasks. The reported numbers show consistent improvements over the OpenVLA-OFT baseline, including LIBERO average SR gains from 96.8 to 98.0 in the multi-suite setting and 97.1 to 98.3 in the per-suite setting.

The ablations in Table 4 support that both state-based initialization and the AVA module contribute to the final performance, and the token-pruning analysis suggests the learned weights capture some task-relevant visual signal.
weaknesses: The central novelty is limited. Conditioning current visual processing on a previous hidden state is a standard recurrent-policy idea, and the POMDP framing is mostly motivational rather than technically developed. The paper does not convincingly establish why this specific AVA design is a substantial conceptual advance over simpler recurrent, frame-stacking, memory-token, or history-conditioned attention baselines.

The empirical gains over the strongest baselines are small on saturated benchmarks and are not accompanied by variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-seed analysis. For example, the LIBERO average gains over OpenVLA-OFT are about 1.2 points, and several per-suite differences are less than or around one point; without statistical evidence, it is hard to judge robustness.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. Many simulation baselines are taken from prior papers rather than reproduced under matched checkpoints, training data, compute, and evaluation conditions. This weakens the state-of-the-art claim, especially because the reported improvements are often marginal.

The ablation suite is incomplete for the main claim. There is no comparison to simple temporal baselines such as concatenating recent frames, adding a GRU/LSTM state, using previous action embeddings, using memory tokens without AVA, or using the same recurrent state without the proposed attention reweighting mechanism beyond the limited component ablation.

The method description has technical ambiguities. The recurrent state shape and action-placeholder formulation are confusing, especially around action chunks and dimensions; the inference section appears to say the forward pass extracts r_{t-1} rather than r_t; and the relationship between action chunking, recurrent updates, and actual control timesteps is underspecified.

The real-world evaluation is useful but small and not sufficiently rigorous. It reports 24-30 trials per task with only two baselines and no uncertainty estimates, and the paper does not make clear whether hyperparameters, demonstrations, and model selection were matched tightly enough to support strong sim-to-real claims.

The paper claims active visual attention improves perception and robustness, but the qualitative heatmaps are mostly illustrative. There is little causal evidence that the highlighted regions are responsible for success, and no failure analysis showing when the attention mechanism helps or hurts.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendix gives many hyperparameters, but important details such as evaluation seeds, exact checkpoint selection, real-world calibration/evaluation protocol, and whether code/checkpoints will be released are missing or unclear.

strengths: The paper addresses a real limitation of current VLA policies: frame-wise visual processing is poorly matched to partially observed, temporally evolving manipulation. The POMDP framing is appropriate, and the proposed recurrent state plus active visual attention mechanism is a coherent way to inject history into visual token weighting and action-placeholder initialization.

The method is technically plausible and clearly specified at the architectural level. The recurrent state is derived from action-related hidden states, the AVA module uses language-conditioned visual features and cross-attention to recurrent state, and the resulting soft weights are integrated into the LLM attention computation.

Empirical coverage is strong. The paper evaluates on LIBERO, CALVIN ABC-to-D, LIBERO+ perturbations, and real-world Mobile ALOHA tasks. Reported results are consistently favorable, including state-of-the-art averages on LIBERO and CALVIN and improved robustness on several LIBERO+ perturbation types.

The ablations are useful: the paper separates the effect of state-based initialization from the AVA module, and also tests multiple backbones on LIBERO-Long. These results support the claim that both proposed components contribute and that the improvement is not limited to one initialization.
The visual-token-pruning analysis provides additional evidence that the learned AVA weights capture task-relevant visual information rather than being only an uninterpretable auxiliary mechanism.

The appendix includes many implementation details, including LoRA settings, sequence length, loss weights, action chunk sizes, training steps, and real-world task protocols, which improves reproducibility relative to many VLA papers.
weaknesses: The absolute gains over the strongest direct baseline, OpenVLA-OFT, are modest on saturated benchmarks: LIBERO improves from 96.8 to 98.0 in the multi-suite setting and 97.1 to 98.3 in the per-suite setting. These gains are meaningful but close to the ceiling, and the paper does not report variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

The real-world evaluation is encouraging but still limited. It compares only against UniVLA and OpenVLA-OFT, uses a small number of trials per task, and does not report run-to-run variability or failure taxonomy. This makes it hard to judge robustness beyond the selected task suite.

The paper relies heavily on comparisons to reported numbers from prior work for simulation benchmarks. Differences in training data, checkpoints, evaluation details, or implementation choices could affect fairness, especially for rapidly evolving VLA baselines.

The novelty is somewhat incremental in architectural terms: recurrent hidden-state conditioning, FiLM/cross-attention, and attention reweighting are established ingredients. The contribution is their integration into VLA visual processing, but the paper’s claim of being the first to address the limitation via a POMDP-inspired approach feels stronger than the evidence warrants given related temporal and memory-based VLA/VLM work.

The recurrent state is motivated as an approximation to a belief state, but the paper does not directly evaluate whether it captures hidden state, occlusion, object permanence, or long-horizon memory beyond downstream success rates and attention visualizations. The theoretical framing is useful but not deeply validated.

Computational tradeoffs are underreported. AVA adds recurrent processing and attention modules, but the paper does not clearly quantify training/inference overhead, latency, memory, or whether token-pruning can recover the added cost in deployed settings.

Some methodological details remain ambiguous for exact reproduction, including seed counts, evaluation episode counts for simulation, details of baseline reimplementation versus copied results, and how recurrent state is handled across action chunks and environment stepping.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of current VLA policies: frame-wise visual processing is weak for partially observable, long-horizon manipulation. The POMDP/recurrent-state framing is well motivated and leads to a concrete architectural change rather than only a conceptual argument.

The proposed method is technically plausible and reasonably simple: a recurrent state derived from previous action-related hidden states is used both to initialize action placeholders and to modulate visual-token attention through the AVA module. This makes the contribution easy to understand and potentially useful for other VLA backbones.

The empirical coverage is strong. The paper evaluates on LIBERO, CALVIN ABC->D, LIBERO+ robustness perturbations, and real-world Mobile ALOHA tasks. Improvements are consistent across many settings, including long-horizon CALVIN chains where the gains over OpenVLA-OFT are substantial.

The ablations are meaningful. The paper separates state-based initialization from the AVA module, tests different backbones, studies token pruning, analyzes the regularizer, and includes an appendix comparison under matched training settings to address the concern that improvements might come only from extra training.

The manuscript is generally clear, with equations, architecture diagrams, implementation details, and qualitative attention visualizations that help explain what the recurrent attention mechanism is doing.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. Recurrent hidden-state conditioning, POMDP motivation, FiLM/cross-attention modulation, and token reweighting are all familiar ingredients; the paper's contribution is mainly their integration into an OpenVLA-OFT-style VLA pipeline. The claim of being the first to explicitly address history via a POMDP-inspired VLA approach feels somewhat overstated given related recurrent, memory, and history-aware robotic/VLA work.

Several reported improvements on LIBERO are small and occur on a saturated benchmark. For example, average success improves from 96.8 to 98.0 in the all-suite setting and from 97.1/97.5 to 98.2 in the per-suite setting. These gains are consistent, but the paper does not report variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, making it hard to judge robustness of the smaller margins.

The main training protocol may still confound architecture and optimization. The method is initialized from a post-trained OpenVLA-OFT checkpoint and trained further; the matched-training appendix helps, but it is only shown for LIBERO and not for CALVIN or real-world tasks, where the strongest claims about generality and transfer are made.

The real-world evaluation is useful but limited. It uses only two reproduced baselines, small numbers of evaluation trials, and no uncertainty estimates. The tasks demonstrate promise, but the evidence is not strong enough to fully support broad claims of real-world generalization.

The recurrent-state design is not deeply analyzed. The state is derived from previous hidden states rather than an explicit belief update over observations and executed actions, and training uses a short unroll with detachment while inference runs recurrently over entire episodes. The paper acknowledges belief drift, but more quantitative analysis of drift, failure modes over horizon length, and sensitivity to initial errors would strengthen the technical case.

The attention/pruning analysis supports interpretability and possible efficiency, but the paper does not report actual latency, memory, or throughput gains. Since the AVA module modifies attention across all LLM layers and adds modules, the compute-overhead claim is not fully substantiated by wall-clock measurements.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and architectural details are given, but the manuscript does not provide code or a complete project link in the extracted text, does not report seeds or standard deviations, and relies on many baseline numbers from original papers that may use different evaluation details.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of current VLA policies: frame-wise visual processing can be inadequate for partially observable, long-horizon manipulation tasks.

The proposed AVA-VLA design is technically plausible: a recurrent hidden state is used both to initialize action placeholders and to modulate visual-token attention, which is a reasonable way to inject execution history into an OpenVLA-OFT-style model.

The empirical section is broad in surface coverage, including LIBERO, CALVIN, LIBERO+ perturbations, several backbone variants, module ablations, pruning analysis, and a small real-robot Mobile ALOHA evaluation.

The ablations generally support that both state-based initialization and the AVA module contribute to the reported gains, and the matched-training appendix helps address one obvious compute-confounding concern.
weaknesses: The main contribution is not very original relative to recurrent policies, memory-augmented VLAs, token reweighting/pruning, FiLM/cross-attention modulation, and POMDP-motivated belief-state approximations. The POMDP framing mostly motivates a standard recurrent hidden-state mechanism rather than yielding a substantially new technical formulation.

The evidence is weaker than the claims of broad state-of-the-art performance suggest. On saturated LIBERO settings, the gains over OpenVLA-OFT are small, e.g. 96.8 to 98.0 average in the one-policy setting and 97.1 to 98.2 in the per-suite setting, with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance analysis.

Most benchmark baselines appear to be copied from published results rather than reproduced under a unified protocol. This makes the SOTA comparisons difficult to interpret, especially when small differences decide the ranking.

The real-world evaluation is too small and under-specified to strongly support transfer claims: only four task suites with 24-30 trials each are reported, without statistical uncertainty, failure taxonomy, or matched compute/training controls comparable to the simulation appendix.

Several technical details remain ambiguous despite the appendix, including how sequence-valued language features are reduced for FiLM, the exact recurrent-state update used across action chunks, the dimensional choices for the AVA projections, and the runtime/latency cost of applying attention modulation throughout the LLM.

The method may be confounded by using strong OpenVLA-OFT checkpoints as initialization in the main experiments, and although the appendix includes a matched LIBERO comparison, this control is not extended to CALVIN or the real-world setting.

The attention visualizations are qualitative and not sufficient evidence that the module truly learns task-relevant active perception; no quantitative localization, occlusion, counterfactual history, or history-shuffling analysis is provided to verify the claimed mechanism.

Reproducibility is incomplete: important experimental details such as seed counts, evaluation randomness, hardware cost, wall-clock training/inference overhead, and release status are missing or unclear, and the project-page line in the abstract appears blank.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of current VLA policies: treating each visual observation independently despite manipulation being partially observable and history-dependent. The recurrent-state formulation and its use both for action-token initialization and active visual attention are well motivated for long-horizon robotic control.

The proposed method is technically plausible and cleanly integrated into a strong OpenVLA-OFT baseline. The attention reweighting mechanism is described with sufficient architectural detail, and the training/inference procedure is mostly clear.

Empirical results are strong across multiple settings. AVA-VLA improves over OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, CALVIN ABC->D, LIBERO+ perturbations, and real-world Mobile ALOHA tasks, with especially convincing gains on long-horizon CALVIN sequences and LIBERO-Long.

The ablation evidence is better than typical: the paper separates state-based initialization from the AVA module, evaluates across different backbones, includes CALVIN module ablations, tests matched training compute, studies the regularizer, and explores visual token pruning.

The real-robot evaluation, while not huge, adds useful evidence that the method is not only a simulator benchmark optimization. The qualitative attention visualizations and failure cases also help readers understand the model behavior and limitations.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate rather than transformative. Recurrent state, memory/history conditioning, FiLM-style modulation, and visual-token reweighting are all established ideas; the contribution is mainly a sensible combination tailored to VLA rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle. The POMDP framing is useful motivation, but it does not yield a rigorously analyzed belief-state update.

Some headline comparisons rely on reported numbers from prior work rather than uniformly re-run baselines under identical data, training, hardware, and evaluation protocols. This is common in robotics papers, but it weakens claims of state-of-the-art performance, especially when gains on saturated LIBERO metrics are often around 1 point.

The statistical reliability of the results is underreported. The paper gives success rates but no confidence intervals, seeds, or variance. This matters for LIBERO where scores are near ceiling, and for real-robot experiments where the number of trials per task is modest.

The real-world evaluation is encouraging but still limited: only two baselines are compared, the task set is small, and there is no analysis of failure frequency across object/layout variations or whether the recurrent state causes recovery versus drift in practice.

Compute and deployment costs are not fully characterized. The paper states that added parameters are under 1%, and token pruning is explored, but it does not report latency, memory, throughput, or whether AVA attention modulation over all LLM layers affects real-time control.

The method has several hyperparameters and design choices whose sensitivity is unclear, including recurrent-state dimensionality, truncation length T=4, detach point, gamma values, regularization target c, and the choice of previous action hidden states. A horizon/sensitivity study would strengthen reproducibility and scientific understanding.

Interpretability claims from attention visualizations should be treated cautiously. The visual focus maps are suggestive, but the paper does not establish that they are causally responsible for decisions beyond the pruning and ablation evidence.

Reproducibility is decent in terms of described training settings, but still incomplete: the abstract's project page appears blank in the extracted manuscript, code/release status is unclear, and important evaluation details such as random seeds and exact trial protocols are not fully specified.
